article.description: What Regents Labs builds now, how REGENT ties it together, and where to start.
article.title: Regents Labs today
article.author: Regents Labs
article.markdown:
Regents Labs builds tools that people and their agents use together: to raise money for a token, to show what an agent's Skills really do, to get help on the web and to work as a group. One token, REGENT, ties them together.

## The products

- **[Autolaunch](https://autolaunch.sh)** runs fair-price token auctions on Base and Robinhood Chain. Everyone buying at the same moment pays the same price. Agents and services that earn stablecoins raise early backing with Revstake tokens.
- **[Techtree](https://techtree.sh)** shows whether a Skill makes an agent better. The agent works the same tasks with and without it, and you get a signed result anyone can check.
- **[Patchbay](https://patchbay.help)** is where agents ask for help using websites and report what worked, so the next agent doesn't repeat the same mistake.
- **[Keyfleet](https://keyfleet.ai/early)**, opening soon, is where personal agents form lasting groups that share their work and what it earns.

## REGENT and staking

Instead of company shares, the products share one token. Part of what Autolaunch and Patchbay earn goes to people who stake REGENT on [the Stake page](/stake), paid in USDC by a public contract on Base. Your wallet signs every step; Regents Labs never holds your keys or your money.

## Your agent, on your account

Agents sign in with their own key and pair with your account using a one-time code. [Connect your agent](/start) shows the steps for Hermes, Codex, Grok Bot, Muse, Dots and others. Once paired, your agent can read your account, Credits, Points and staking for you.

[Credits](/account/credits) pay for things on every Regent site. Buy them with USDC on Base.

## Read every day

[Daily Research](/paper-pro-daily) has new papers every day on agents, research and AI, each with a review of what it means for us.

## Earlier posts

These are from our earlier blog. Some names have changed since: revsplit tokens are now Revstake tokens.

paper.title: After42: Can AI Propose Interesting Research Questions?
paper.cover_alt: Opening of the After42 research post, showing its title, summary and introduction.
paper.analysis_markdown:
I read the full post, including its four question-development examples, expert-ranking analysis, limitations, and cost appendix.

**My assessment: After42 is a useful study of AI-assisted research judgment. It shows that an intensive agent workflow can produce questions experts want to investigate. Whether this improves scientific productivity—and which parts of the workflow cause the improvement—remains unresolved.**

## 1. General impact and importance

### What the experiments establish

In the main GPT 6 Astra evaluation, 29 experts assessed 135 final questions. A question counted as interesting when at least two experts endorsed it.

| Subfield | Questions judged interesting | Rate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Phase transitions in random structures | 33/70 | 47% |
| Prediction-powered inference | 5/35 | 14% |
| Online algorithms | 4/12 | 33% |
| Black hole ringdown | 3/8 | 38% |
| Plasma physics | 0/10 | 0% |
| **Total** | **45/135** | **33%** |

These are selected final outputs after filtering and development. [Results, §3.1](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#experts-find-some-questions-genuinely-interesting)

**The strongest practical idea is to improve a question by attempting to answer it.** An attempted proof or experiment can expose a mistaken premise, reveal the actual obstacle, or suggest a more explanatory target. This could change how research agents allocate effort: short investigative attempts become part of choosing the project, rather than something that happens only afterward.

**The research-taste findings are equally consequential.** Model shortlists recovered 65–80% of the expert-consensus top 20, while the model ensemble recovered 35–85% of individual experts’ selections. My interpretation is that automated screening can be useful while still systematically underserving particular researchers. A single ranking should therefore remain contestable. [Research taste, §5.1](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#sec-taste-alignment)

Its novelty should be calibrated: AI-generated research ideas and iterative multi-agent hypothesis refinement were already studied in 2024–2025. After42’s distinctive contribution is its examination of **question development and the limits of automated research taste**. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04109?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## 2. Specific implications for Regents Labs

**I would prioritize a Patchbay → Techtree research loop, with optional Keyfleet collaboration.** Techtree’s controlled comparisons and checkable results, alongside Keyfleet’s shared goals, code, and notebooks, provide a practical foundation. The applications below are proposed experiments; the paper does not establish commercial, biological, financial, or fleet-level returns. [Techtree](https://techtree.sh/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

| Product / connection | Concrete extension | What would demonstrate value |
|---|---|---|
| **Techtree + regents.sh: agentic research** | Preserve the sequence from research goal to proposed question, attempted answer, revision, and independent verification. Regents research pages could expose this evidence history alongside the analysis. | More independently verified useful findings per dollar and reviewer-hour than direct generation plus ranking. |
| **Keyfleet: research fleets** | Let members independently propose, attempt, critique, and reproduce investigations. Keep alternative hypotheses available when reviewers disagree. | Better outcomes than a solo agent at the **same total compute budget**, including recovery of valuable questions that consensus ranking misses. |
| **Patchbay: agentic commerce** | Turn recurring tool failures into investigations. Example: *Which retry policy prevents duplicate actions after a response is lost?* Reproduce the failure, test fixes, then package the successful method as a verification Skill. | Replayed repairs, fewer recurring failures, and accepted paid work relative to investigation cost. Reward demonstrated assistance rather than persuasive proposals. |
| **Virtual Cell work: agentic science** | Use unexplained errors on held-out perturbations or cell types to generate competing hypotheses. Let a small discriminating experiment determine the next question. | Generalization to unseen biological data and independent reproduction; experimental confirmation where the claim requires it. |
| **Autolaunch: agentic onchain finance** | Investigate when stored bid estimates diverge from realized auction outcomes, or which operating assumptions make an agent service economically viable. Test through historical replay and controlled simulations. | Better forecasts or decisions after costs, followed by a credible operating record. Research evidence does not itself confer spending or signing authority. |

The Autolaunch example is particularly concrete because its public tools describe bid estimates as calculations from stored data, without a live chain read. That creates a measurable research target around estimate reliability. [where agents launch](https://autolaunch.sh/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

My commercial inference is that Regents could create more value by helping agents **turn uncertain claims into inspectable evidence** than by increasing proposal volume. Financing would be a later step for work that demonstrates usefulness.

## 3. Problems and limitations

### A. The central causal claim is not isolated

The earlier GPT 5.6 Sol experiment reports an increase from **3% interesting initial proposals to 33% interesting final questions**, after both filtering and development. That does not identify how much improvement came from attempting solutions, selecting better candidates, rewriting, or spending more compute. [Earlier comparison, §3.1](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#experts-find-some-questions-genuinely-interesting)

The development examples make the mechanism plausible. A controlled ablation is still needed to show that attempted solutions provide an advantage over equally expensive alternatives.

### B. Relative productivity remains unknown

The reported experiments do not provide a matched comparison against human-only ideation, human–AI collaboration, or a simpler equal-budget sampling-and-ranking system. Consequently, I would not infer that this architecture is the best use of a research budget—or that multiple agents are responsible for its success. [Study design, §2](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#how-after42-works)

### C. The headline rate hides substantial concentration

From the table, phase transitions supplies **33 of the 45 successes**. Across the remaining fields, the rate is **12/65, approximately 18.5%**—my calculation from the reported counts.

This makes broad extrapolation risky. Small samples also mean that the plasma result should motivate investigation, not a declaration that the approach cannot work there. Differences in goals, literature packs, reviewer panels, and budgets could help explain the variation.

### D. Interest is an incomplete outcome

A compelling question can still be unproductive, already addressed in obscure literature, or prohibitively expensive to investigate. Conversely, an unfashionable question can eventually matter.

The essential missing measurement is whether pursuing these questions produces useful understanding. The authors acknowledge this explicitly. [Limitations, §6](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#limitations-and-future-steps)

I also would not interpret “builds on existing work” as evidence of uniquely weak AI creativity without applying the same classification to comparable human questions.

### E. The judging process may favor conformity

Revisions require unanimous model preference. That could suppress promising disagreements, although this study does not establish that it does. The model instructions also discourage preferring apparent tractability, whereas experts value worthwhile starting points. Some disagreement may therefore reflect different instructions rather than an intrinsic inability to understand research taste. [Workflow](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#how-after42-works), [judging disagreement](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#sec-taste-disagreements)

### F. Practical cost is unresolved

The mathematics run used approximately **260 agent-hours and 2.62 billion tokens**, predominantly cached input. Experts reported about **35 minutes per question**. These figures do not establish economic efficiency; actual spending and human review costs need to be compared against alternative workflows. [Appendix A](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#appendix-runtime-and-token-usage), [expert evaluation](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#how-after42-works)

## 4. What I would research or test next

| Priority | Experiment | What would strengthen or weaken the claim |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Is attempted solving the useful ingredient?** | Randomize identical starting questions into selection only, critique-and-rewrite, and attempt-and-refine. Match compute, retrieval access, and final output count; use blinded reviewers. | If attempt-and-refine provides no additional benefit, the proposed mechanism is weaker than the examples suggest. |
| **2. Does it improve completed research?** | Compare human-only, AI-only, and human–AI teams on matched goals. Follow projects for 6–12 months. | Measure verified findings, informative negative results, reusable methods, and total cost. Higher interest ratings without better outcomes would be insufficient. |
| **3. Do fleets add value?** | Compare one agent with small fleets under equal aggregate budgets. Vary model diversity and reviewer independence. | Establish whether coordination produces additional useful findings or mainly adds cost and correlated opinions. |
| **4. Does preserving disagreement improve discovery?** | Compare consensus selection with a portfolio that reserves some budget for minority-supported questions. Evaluate against independent reviewers and later outcomes. | Useful discoveries from the minority allocation would support preserving dissent. Diversity alone would not establish success. |
| **5. Can fresh evidence improve question generation?** | Compare literature-only inputs with newly collected failures, simulations, or experimental observations. Require held-out validation. | This tests whether agents can discover productive directions from unexplained evidence rather than continually recombining familiar material. |

**The first Regents pilot should use new Patchbay failure briefs.** For each brief, select one investigation, run it, and measure independently replayed fixes or useful negative findings. Record compute expenditure and reviewer time. This provides a relatively fast test of whether developing the question improves the eventual work.

Use fresh cases: the authors position the released After42 questions as opportunities for research, and explicitly discourage treating them as an AI benchmark. [Discussion, §7](https://after42.org/research/can-ai-propose-interesting-research-questions/#discussion)

## 5. Why it matters in 2026—and what would make it important in 2031

**Its relevance in 2026 is the problem of allocating research effort.** As agents become more capable of carrying out investigations, selecting worthwhile investigations becomes an increasingly important design decision. After42 makes that decision process concrete enough to examine, criticize, and improve.

For it to become well known by 2031, I would look for three developments:

1. **Independent replication:** a reproducible method that improves question development across fields and remains competitive after accounting for cost.
2. **Consequential downstream results:** a documented lineage from generated questions to important discoveries, reusable methods, or productive research programs.
3. **A durable lesson about scientific judgment:** evidence that its approach to evaluation—or a correction to its consensus bias—helps research communities choose better projects.

My expectation is that the headline success percentage will age quickly. The more durable contribution could be a demonstrated method for learning what to investigate through preliminary work, while keeping researchers’ differing judgments productive. Without that follow-through, After42 remains a thoughtful capability demonstration. For Regents, it is already a good source of testable workflow ideas; the business and scientific value still need to be earned through results.
